new_keys.key: Stage the clutch: in gear, ease the lever out until the bike just starts to creep, then pull it back a touch so you sit right at the bite point when the gate drops.
Fingers: some coaches run three fingers on the clutch with the index finger on the grip to hold the body forward; others use two. Pick one and keep it the same every start.
Meter drive with the clutch, not the throttle: hold steady revs and use the lever to control wheelspin and front lift; it reacts faster than the throttle.
Aim for a front wheel just skimming a few inches up; no lift at all usually means there was more drive to use, a big wheelie means slip the clutch or ease off.
Brief ease of drive as the rear tire crosses the gate slot, then full drive once it is on the dirt.
Eyes: rest them on a spot just in front of the gate so the drop shows in peripheral vision; do not stare at the gate for long before it falls.
Rut behind the gate: level, packed and straight, front wheel aligned with it, rear centered; no ramp shape and no deep hole.
Grippy pad: lean forward with elbows high, lock the legs and core so the hips cannot slide back. Slippery pad: torso more upright, smoother throttle and clutch, both feet down for balance.

Concrete: sweep the spot clean, keep throttle low (roughly a quarter to half), release the clutch gently until the rear reaches dirt, then get forward and on the gas. A holeshot device is generally not used on concrete.
Get the feet onto the pegs quickly once driving; the first shift timing depends on the surface (too early in mud bogs the bike).

new_faults.fault: Hips slide back off the drop
new_faults.looks_like: Rear of the seat under the rider in the first metres, front climbing.
new_faults.why: No leg and core lock on a grippy pad; arms holding the rider on.
new_faults.fix: Lock heels and knees against the bike, chest forward, elbows high before the drop.
new_faults.drill: Film side-on starts and check hip position on the seat at the first frame of motion.

new_faults.fault: Wheelspin off a slick or concrete pad
new_faults.looks_like: Rear spinning in place, bike slow to move, rear stepping sideways.
new_faults.why: Too many revs or dumped clutch; leaning over the bar pad on a slick start.
new_faults.fix: Fewer revs, gentle clutch, torso more upright to weight the rear; open up once on dirt.
new_faults.drill: Alternate practice starts on a slick and a grippy surface, noting revs used on each.

new_faults.looks_like: Bike surges then bogs, or wheelies then drops.
new_faults.why: Slipping the clutch out partly and then dropping it, or relying on the throttle for control.
new_faults.fix: One smooth, full release from the staged bite point; hold the throttle steady and use the clutch to fine-tune.

new_faults.looks_like: Front lifting early or the bike rolling into the gate before the drop.
new_faults.why: Rut built as a ramp, or a deep hole left behind the gate.
new_faults.fix: Fill and pack the rut level and straight; only build a small lip if the coach or surface calls for it.

new_faults.looks_like: Rider rolls off when the front lifts or body position is imperfect; others drive past.
new_faults.why: Reacting to a small wheelie by closing the throttle.
new_faults.fix: Stay on the gas and correct with body weight and a touch of clutch instead of shutting off.

drills.name: Start every lap
drills.how: At practice, begin each lap or each moto with a start from a gate or line.
drills.progression: Start with clutch release only, then add gate reaction, then add the first turn.
drills.done_when: Starts feel the same every time and are no longer a separate event.

drills.name: Five perfect in a row
drills.how: Count consecutive starts that meet your checklist (body forward, small wheelie, straight, quick feet up); any mistake resets the count to one.
drills.progression: Raise the target count or add a gate and other riders.
drills.done_when: Five clean starts in a row without a reset.

drills.name: Surface pair
drills.how: Do practice starts on both a slick and a grippy surface and note what revs and body position worked for each.
drills.progression: Limit grippy-pad starts to protect the clutch; quality over quantity.
drills.done_when: You can say before the gate which setting you will use for the pad in front of you.

drills.name: Gate timing study
drills.how: Watch earlier motos and count how long the gate takes to fall after the card turns.
drills.progression: Use it to set when you bring revs up.
drills.done_when: You are ready at the bite point every time the gate falls, without anticipating it.

pro_tips.tip: Hold the clutch at the bite point with steady revs; most of the start is clutch and traction, not throttle.
Use the rev-indicator light, where the bike has one, because you cannot hear your own engine on a full gate.
Practise starts a day or session before the race and build belief in a routine; reaction time is less important than what you do once moving.
On concrete, a short controlled spin to clean the tire is better than a long burnout that wears it.
Lightly holding the front brake while bringing the clutch to the bite point keeps the bike still against the gate.
Lighter riders get less grip on a slick gate, so throttle control matters even more for them.

disagreements.point: Feet at the gate: MXA has both feet forward on the pegs, MotoOnline has both feet down, BCP has feet angled about 45 degrees with heels hooked under the pegs on grippy pads and both feet down on slippery ones. The current skill says pegs or one foot ready; treat it as surface- and rider-dependent.
Gear: MXA and MotoOnline use second; Semics says first or second; the current skill already covers taller gears on slick pads.
Rut ramp at the gate: Semics builds a small ramp at the gate for traction; MotoOnline usually skips it except in sand; MXA warns against a ramp-shaped rut.
Rut on faster bikes: MXA keeps the rut on faster bikes for sidewall grip but flattens it for a slow 125 so the rear can spin up.
Shifting: MotoOnline has holeshot riders stay pinned and shift without the clutch to stay in the power; others say short-shift. Clutchless upshifts add drivetrain wear.

new_keys.key: Set the body before the brakes: stand, hips back and a little space between you and the seat so a bump cannot throw you forward, then brake.
Close the throttle fully, then squeeze the front and press the rear progressively to just short of lock-up, both wheels still turning.
Downshift once braking is under control, so you exit in the right gear.
Front does most of the stopping (MXA gives roughly 70 to 80 percent); the rear steers, settles the bike over bumps and helps keep the engine running.
Brake for the entry speed you need, not simply as late as possible; slightly early beats overshooting.
Surface sets the marker: later on grippy loam or grass, earlier and lighter on slick hardpack and off-cambers.
Look further ahead while braking to pick the line with the fewest bumps; a smoother line that lets you brake harder can beat the direct one.
Into a rutted corner, brake standing with the bike fairly upright and lean only once both wheels are tracking in the rut.
Release the rear brake at the transition from braking to drive and put the foot back on the peg; control then comes from clutch, throttle and body.

Engine braking: on a four-stroke keeping the clutch out uses the engine to help slow the bike and loads the front for bite in ruts; pull the clutch in for crawl-speed corners or a brake slide so it does not stall.
Engine braking also stiffens the rear over braking bumps and can make it chatter or hop; downshifting late or pulling the clutch reduces it.
Small braking bumps can be bounced like small whoops; big, spaced ones can be ridden like a rhythm section. Scrub speed before the bumps where you can rather than braking hard through them.
Land from a jump before a turn slightly front-first, let the front settle, then build front brake; braking hard on an unloaded front can tuck it or lift the rear.

new_faults.fault: Braking before the body is set
new_faults.looks_like: Rider upright or weight forward as the fork dives; elbows locked.
new_faults.why: Hitting the brakes before moving back and bracing.
new_faults.fix: Stand, hips back and brace legs first, then brake.
new_faults.drill: Straight-line stops from a marker, filming side-on, checking body position before the first brake frame.

new_faults.looks_like: Rider seated in the braking bumps, bouncing on the seat.
new_faults.why: Tired or habit; sitting early for the turn.
new_faults.fix: Stay standing through braking and sit only as you come off the brakes.

new_faults.looks_like: Rear high, front compressed, rider pitched forward, often after landing on the front wheel or hitting a roller under hard braking.
new_faults.why: Hard front brake while the front is the only wheel down, or braking over a bump.
new_faults.fix: Do the hard braking before the roller or bump, and ease the front brake over a single big bump before reapplying.

new_faults.looks_like: Lap times fade as the moto goes on; rider off the brakes and coasting before the turn.
new_faults.why: Fatigue and losing trust in the front.
new_faults.fix: Use a fixed marker (bale, rock, bump) and keep it each lap.

new_faults.fault: Dragging the rear brake through the corner
new_faults.looks_like: Rear foot still on the pedal past the apex; bike slow to drive; leg kicked out.
new_faults.why: Using the rear brake as a crutch; no roll speed.
new_faults.fix: Come off the rear before or at the transition and let roll speed carry you; get on the gas.
new_faults.drill: Section laps with no rear brake to build roll speed.

new_faults.fault: Rear steps out then straightens repeatedly
new_faults.looks_like: Rear slides, rider lets off, bike straightens and the cycle repeats into the turn.
new_faults.why: Clutch pulled in at speed on a slick approach so there is no engine braking to steady the rear.
new_faults.fix: Keep the clutch out at speed, modulate the rear just short of lock.

new_faults.fault: Too much rear brake making the bike stand up
new_faults.looks_like: Bike standing up and running wide on entry.
new_faults.why: Heavy rear brake or turning in at too sharp an angle.
new_faults.fix: Lighter rear, more front, use the width of the track.

drills.name: Front-only and rear-only stops
drills.how: On a straight, stop to a full halt using only the front, then only the rear.
drills.progression: Start slow and build speed; then mix both brakes; then try different surfaces.
drills.done_when: You can stop at a marker without locking either wheel and know where each one starts to lock on that surface.

drills.name: Half-speed marker
drills.how: Ride one corner at about half speed, find a braking marker, then each lap brake a little later and get on the gas a little sooner.
drills.progression: Move the marker only after the current one is easy.
drills.done_when: Same marker and same entry speed lap after lap.

drills.name: Slow oval release
drills.how: Ride a slow oval and focus only on releasing the rear brake and putting the foot back on the peg at the transition to drive.
drills.progression: Raise speed once it is automatic.
drills.done_when: Foot comes off the pedal at the same spot every lap without thinking.

drills.name: Wheelie to stoppie control (intermediate and up)
drills.how: On flat, grippy ground at walking pace, lift the front slightly with throttle and clutch, bring it down with a tap of rear brake, then a small stoppie with front brake and weight forward, clutch in so it does not stall.
drills.progression: Only the height of the wheelie and stoppie grows with skill; keep both small.
drills.done_when: You can lift and set either wheel smoothly and stop the rear from rising by easing the front brake.

pro_tips.tip: Brake firmly, not gently: timid braking is a common time loss, but squeeze, do not grab.
Braking should flow straight into drive at the transition with no coasting in between.
On rocky or downhill braking use less front and more rear; avoid heavy front brake over loose rocks.
Keep a finger on the clutch while braking so a downshift or a stall-save is instant.
Advanced: a touch of trailing throttle while braking can settle the rear over high-speed braking bumps.

disagreements.point: Clutch while braking: Semics and Dirt Action keep the clutch out to use engine braking and say pulling it fully in removes it; MXA and the current skill pull it in for full braking without stalling, mainly on 125s and four-strokes in tight turns. Both agree on pulling it in at crawl speed.

Throttle while braking: Dirt Action calls trailing throttle an advanced bump technique in one article and lists leaving the throttle partly on as a panic mistake in another; MX-Gear says no clutch while braking. Treat trailing throttle as advanced only.
Rear brake in braking bumps: Semics allows light rear brake with light throttle in big bumps; Swap Moto (Clason) and the braking-bump tip say stay off the brakes and carry roll speed through them.

Weight while braking: Dirt Action and Josh Green say weight back; the current skill says hips back over the pegs, not on the fender. These fit if "back" means hips back while standing, not sitting on the rear.
Front/rear split: MXA gives about 70 percent front; the MXA drills article says the rear gives about 20 percent; exact numbers vary by surface and are rough guides only.

new_keys.key: Enter with a small arc from slightly outside (a foot or two) rather than driving straight at the rut.
Lift the inside leg high and clear before leaning in, knee slightly bent, foot near the fork leg, toe angled so a touching boot slides instead of digging in.
Ball of the outside foot on the peg, outside knee pressing the bike; that keeps the tires pressed into the rut and stops the brake-side foot hitting the rear brake.
Use the throttle to correct lean in the rut: a little more if the bike is dropping too low or starting to lowside, a little less if it is standing up and climbing.
Choose the exit gear before entry; many coaches favour a taller gear with low revs so the bike lugs calmly through.
Read how far over to lean from how high other riders' tire marks sit on the rut wall; taller, firmer walls take more lean and need the leg higher.
Steady in, fast out: settle with the leg clear and eyes on the exit before applying power; slip the clutch a little on exit to drive hard without a wheelie.
Exit obstacles in the rut (roots, bumps): ease off before the rear reaches them, sit the bike up early, then get back on the power once it lands.
Off-camber ruts: slower, more patient entry, inside foot lower and flatter to help stabilise.
Engine braking on a four-stroke helps the front stay in a hard, rutted turn; on soft dirt less of it keeps the front from diving.

new_faults.looks_like: Rear wheel hopping or popping out of the rut; bike standing up mid-turn.
new_faults.why: Using the rear brake while leaned over in the rut.
new_faults.fix: Finish braking before the rut; if needed, a light front brake drag keeps the front planted.
new_faults.drill: Rut circles with no rear brake.

new_faults.looks_like: Bike rising and dropping in the rut, rider correcting with the bars.
new_faults.why: On-off throttle bursts.
new_faults.fix: Hold a steady throttle and adjust it only to correct the lean.
new_faults.drill: Throttle trailing laps through one rut.

new_faults.looks_like: Front knifes into the rut after the rider rolls off mid-rut.
new_faults.why: Closing the throttle mid-rut adds engine braking and loads the front.
new_faults.fix: Keep a little throttle on; use a touch of clutch to keep moving rather than backing off.

new_faults.looks_like: Rider standing up or dabbing mid-rut, bike stalling or falling in.
new_faults.why: Over-braking before the rut and then trying to build speed in it.
new_faults.fix: Enter with enough speed to carry through; set throttle while braking so entry needs no big change.
new_faults.drill: Start on short, shallow ruts and move to longer, deeper ones.

new_faults.fault: Leaning with no pressure on the pegs
new_faults.looks_like: Rider and bike leaned together, tires skating, little control if it slips.
new_faults.why: Weight on the seat and inside, not on the outside peg.
new_faults.fix: Weight the outside peg and outside knee so the tires stay pressed into the rut.

new_faults.looks_like: Inside boot touching down repeatedly, front tucking.
new_faults.why: Habit or nerves.
new_faults.fix: Keep the inside leg up and leading; only dab when you truly need balance.

new_faults.fault: Hitting roots with the front leaned over
new_faults.looks_like: Front pushed wide or tucked at the rut exit.
new_faults.why: Crossing a root while still leaned.
new_faults.fix: Sit the bike up before the obstacle, coast over angled roots with the front light.

drills.name: Throttle trailing
drills.how: Ride a single rut repeatedly holding a smooth, steady throttle; change it only to fix lean.
drills.progression: Shallow rut first, then deeper, then longer.
drills.done_when: The bike stays at a steady height in the rut and exits without a bar correction.

drills.name: Gear call
drills.how: Before each rut, say the entry and exit gear and check them on the approach.
drills.progression: Try one gear taller than usual.
drills.done_when: No shift needed in or right after the rut.

drills.name: Rut circles
drills.how: Ride circles in a rutted turn without the rear brake; drag the front lightly if sliding out. Do it with one leg forward, then both feet on the pegs, then standing.
drills.progression: Small then big circles; move through the three stances.
drills.done_when: Smooth circles in each stance without the rear brake.

drills.name: Rut track no brakes, no clutch
drills.how: Ride a short rut track with laps that use no brakes and laps that use no clutch.
drills.progression: Slow to feel the flow, then build pace.
drills.done_when: You can lap it at a steady pace without either control.

pro_tips.tip: Look at the exit as soon as you are in the entry, not at the front fender; the bike follows the eyes.
Keep the head over the front third of the bike; falling back over the rear is the classic rut mistake.
Accept a little mid-turn speed for a cleaner exit in technical ruts.
Practise ruts instead of avoiding them; they get easier only with reps.
Where ruts cross at the exit, keep the front light with a little power and set it down where it does not break your flow.

disagreements.point: Sit or stand into the rut: MXA says stay standing as long as you can; ADB and Dirt Action sit early (a few metres before) with the leg up. The current skill says sit forward.

Lean the body or not: Racer X and Dirt Action lean head and upper body into the turn with the bike; Keegan says tilt the bike under you rather than leaning with it; BCP says match the bike angle in ruts and berms. Upper body stays over the bike in all of them.

Brakes in the rut: the current skill says brake before the rut, not in it; MXA (advanced), Keegan and Damian Smith allow a light front brake drag through the first part of tight ruts. All agree no rear brake in the rut.
Gear: MXA and ADB favour a taller gear lugging; Keegan only says choose the exit gear beforehand.

new_keys.key: Brake hard standing and in a straight line, then move from standing to seated in one smooth motion as you release the brakes; drop onto the seat gently, not with a thump.
Some coaches release the rear first but keep a little front brake as you sit to settle the front, then come off it before the lean.
Enter wide, cut to the inside at the apex and let momentum carry you out wide on exit.
Sit on the outside edge of the seat and press the outside peg with the ball of the foot, toes down; keep the upper body upright over the bike.
Light on the bars: a tense grip makes the front push; relaxed arms let the bike drift safely.
Throttle comes in gently from about mid-corner; steady throttle turns the bike better than brake.
On exit pick the bike up, move back on the seat for rear grip and build to full throttle smoothly.
Hardpack sweepers: a small controlled drift is fast; a big sideways slide is not.

new_faults.fault: Front pushes from a tight grip
new_faults.looks_like: Front tire scrubbing wide, rider stiff with elbows locked.
new_faults.why: Tension on the bars and too much entry speed.
new_faults.fix: Relax the grip, slow entry slightly, weight the outside peg.

new_faults.fault: Braking in the turn instead of before
new_faults.looks_like: Front tucks right at turn-in.
new_faults.why: Still on the brakes while leaning.
new_faults.fix: Finish braking upright, then lean.

new_faults.looks_like: Bike jolts or wiggles as the rider sits.
new_faults.why: Abrupt sit-down unloading and reloading the tires.
new_faults.fix: Sit in one smooth move as the brakes come off.

new_faults.fault: Rear spins on exit from clutch feathering
new_faults.looks_like: Rear spinning, bike slow despite noise.
new_faults.why: Feathering the clutch on exit so the tire breaks loose.
new_faults.fix: Roll the throttle on smoothly at the edge of grip; use less clutch.

drills.name: Cone turn track
drills.how: Set a cone on flat ground and ride laps around it practising the stand-to-sit transition and where to look.
drills.progression: Tighter radius, then figure eights, then both directions.
drills.done_when: Smooth stand-to-sit at the same spot every lap with the eyes on the exit.

drills.how: Ride the same flat corner at about half, three-quarter and near race pace in turn.
drills.progression: Move up a step only when the slower one is clean.
drills.done_when: Race pace looks like the 50 percent version, just faster.

drills.name: Powerslide circles (once grip is solid)
drills.how: On a flat, open, smooth area, slide the rear around a circle using seated body position and measured throttle.
drills.progression: Seated first, then standing with both feet on the pegs.
drills.done_when: You can hold a small slide and stop it with the throttle at will.

pro_tips.tip: Flat turns are not a rest spot; more speed makes the front push harder, so stay smooth and patient on the gas.
Watch other riders' lines in flat turns, and decide your line early as bumps build.

disagreements.point: Clutch on exit: Shane Watts says do not feather it, it spins the rear; Sean Hamblin says feather it to control traction rather than dumping it.
Upper body: Hamblin leans the upper body back a little to balance weight; Sleeter leans the head forward over the bars; the current skill keeps the body upright.
Inside foot: most keep it up and forward; Childress (hardpack/Baja style) lets it skim the ground for balance.

skills.note: New id; currently covered inside cornering_flat. Can merge into cornering_flat instead.

new_keys.key: Slow more than for a normal corner and brake a bit earlier; gravity pulls you down the slope. Use a light touch on both brakes, and especially little rear.
Carry rolling speed in, so the rear does not drop away when you get back on the gas.
Sit or crouch toward the outside (downhill) side, upper body upright and level; load the downhill peg as hard as you can and let the bike lean beneath you.
Wait longer than usual for the throttle, then hold it steady; on-off throttle makes the tires slip downhill.
Look ahead at a point on the far side or the top, not at the ground in front.
If there is a rut, aim for its inside edge on entry so the rear does not miss it, and accelerate only once both wheels are in it.
Off-camber uphill: keep the front light and aimed slightly uphill of the main line so the rear stays out of the loose dirt on the downhill side.

new_faults.looks_like: Bike standing up and drifting down the hill.
new_faults.why: Eyes on the ground just ahead.
new_faults.fix: Pick a target on the far side and keep the eyes on it.

new_faults.looks_like: Rear steps out downhill on exit.
new_faults.why: Getting on the gas at the usual point.
new_faults.fix: Wait longer, then roll on steadily.

new_faults.fault: Too much rear brake on an off-camber
new_faults.looks_like: Rear sliding downhill on entry.
new_faults.why: Rear brake used as on a flat turn.
new_faults.fix: Brake earlier and lighter, mostly front, upright.

pro_tips.tip: A slower entry that stays locked into the rut beats a fast one that slides off the camber.

disagreements.point: Seat or crouch: Andrew Short and Nathan Woods sit toward the downhill side; Shane Watts crouches and stays centered front to back while loading the downhill peg so hard the inside foot may lift.

new_keys.key: Lean with the bike in a berm (unlike a flat turn); shoulders over hips, bend at the core rather than folding forward at the hips.
Release the brakes and sit with the leg out a little earlier than feels natural: it carries more speed, gives time to set up and allows a taller gear.
Start the roll-on a little before the point where you would go full throttle, and keep weight forward as you open it.
Do not hit the apex too early: turn in, then straighten so you can get on the gas sooner.
Keep weight low and centered; weight carried high pushes the bike up the berm and delays the exit.
If the bike starts to stand up or climb the berm, quick nips of the clutch cut drive faster than the throttle.
Squaring a berm: you do not have to ride the whole thing; turn sharply off it, point the bike, stand it up and drive. Useful to pass or avoid a hole.
Landing into a turn: decide berm or inside before the jump; the berm is longer but easier to carry speed through, the inside is shorter and harder.

new_faults.fault: Braking late then grabbing throttle and clutch mid-berm
new_faults.looks_like: Bike lurches or stands up halfway round.
new_faults.why: Still braking at turn-in, then trying to make up speed in the turn.
new_faults.fix: Sit and release the brakes earlier, then roll on early and smoothly.

new_faults.looks_like: Head low over the bars, back rounded, weight too far forward.
new_faults.why: Bending at the hips instead of the core.
new_faults.fix: Shoulders over hips, bend through the core.

new_faults.looks_like: Inside leg straight and rigid, boot catching the berm face.
new_faults.why: Bracing with the leg.
new_faults.fix: Slight knee bend, toe pointed so the sole runs parallel to the ground and slides if it touches.

new_faults.fault: Under-leaning and leaning the body out
new_faults.looks_like: Bike too upright, rider hanging the upper body outward.
new_faults.why: Not trusting the berm.
new_faults.fix: Lean the bike more and keep the body with it.

drills.name: Ten clean in a row
drills.how: Pick one berm and ride it until you nail it ten times in a row; any mistake restarts the count.
drills.progression: Then push the entry a little faster with a safe runoff.
drills.done_when: Ten consecutive clean laps of that berm.

drills.name: Many reps of one turn
drills.how: Repeat the same forgiving berm 30 to 50 times, pushing slightly each time: enter a bit faster, hold the line longer, brake later.
drills.progression: Only on a turn with safe runoff.
drills.done_when: You know where the edge is without crashing.

pro_tips.tip: Get on the power sooner, not harder.
Coming off the berm, let the bike drift toward the outside on exit.
If an inside line off a jump goes wrong, run wide to the berm early, even just its end, rather than forcing it.

disagreements.point: Entry: MX-Gear (credited to Catanzaro) says either come off the rear brake and coast in, or brake to the transition and get straight on the gas, and to try both; Racer X Corners and Semics say no coasting at the transition.

skills.note: Corner line-choice additions; race_lines already covers rut choice as the track changes.

new_keys.key: Tight 180s: come in from the outside, cut to the inside and let the bike run wide on exit, a U shape.
Off a jump into a turn the line is fixed in the air: choose it before the face.
Plan a corner several moves ahead and decide your approach before you reach it.
Use the full track width to slow down; drifting wide out of one turn can close the entry to the next.
Pick lines around loose rocks and the trough where they collect, especially on downhills.

new_faults.fault: Butchering the corner after a jump
new_faults.looks_like: Good jump, then over-braking or running wide into the next turn.
new_faults.why: All attention on the jump, none on the turn.
new_faults.fix: Choose the turn line before the jump and spot the landing early.

new_faults.looks_like: Rider turns in early and has to stop mid-turn.
new_faults.why: Cutting the entry for the shortest line.
new_faults.fix: Enter wider, use the track width, and aim for a better exit.

pro_tips.tip: Try lines you are not used to in practice; fast riders keep testing.

skills.note: New id for body position and outside-foot/peg weighting across corners; complements fundamentals.seated_position.

new_keys.key: Load the outside peg from turn-in to exit: release the rear brake, press through the leg and the ball of the foot, toes angled in, and keep pressure through the exit.
Brace the outside knee against the tank to load the peg; do not prop yourself up on a straight, locked leg.
Outside peg pressure matters most on hardpack (rear bite), in ruts (stability), over acceleration bumps (keeps you from bouncing off the seat) and at higher speed.
Rotate through the hips rather than rounding the back; it gives more leverage on the pegs.
Ride on the balls of the feet with toes pointing in so the knees can grip.
Seat position moves with the job: forward to turn and for front grip, a little back when the rear may spin under hard drive.
Weight shifts with the controls: braking pushes weight forward, so move back; accelerating pushes it back, so move forward.
Initiate the turn with the outside shoulder and elbow (Ryan Hughes video title; detail not readable).
Keep the fingers resting on the clutch and front brake, not all four on the grip, especially in a pack.

new_faults.looks_like: Both boots off the pegs mid-corner, bike skating.
new_faults.why: Nerves, or no outside peg habit.
new_faults.fix: Keep the outside foot loaded on the peg; only the inside foot comes off.
new_faults.drill: Laps with both feet on the pegs through every corner.

new_faults.looks_like: Rider thrown up off the seat over exit chop.
new_faults.why: Weight on the seat, not the pegs.
new_faults.fix: Push weight into the outside peg and grip with the knees.

new_faults.fault: Sitting too far back in turns
new_faults.looks_like: Rider mid-seat or behind, front pushing.
new_faults.why: Habit, or reacting to the bike.
new_faults.fix: Sit an inch or two farther forward and get more weight over the bike.
new_faults.drill: Note where you sit in practice and move forward an inch or two.

new_faults.fault: Toes out, knees off the bike
new_faults.looks_like: Gap between knees and bike, toes splayed.
new_faults.why: Feet turned out so the knees cannot close.
new_faults.fix: Turn the toes in; the knees then grip the tank.
new_faults.drill: Knee-grip test standing off the bike.

drills.name: Outside peg laps
drills.how: On a track you know, ride laps focusing only on loading the outside peg in every corner.
drills.progression: Then laps keeping both feet on the pegs to feel the difference.
drills.done_when: Outside foot never comes off the peg and you feel the rear bite on exit.

drills.name: Knee-grip test
drills.how: Stand with feet peg-width apart, toes out, try to touch your knees; then turn the toes in and try again.
drills.progression: Carry the toes-in feel onto the bike.
drills.done_when: Knees reach the tank easily with toes in.

drills.name: Full standing lap
drills.how: After standing circle drills, ride a whole lap standing.
drills.progression: Stand through rough chop and transitions first.
drills.done_when: A full lap standing without the arms tiring.

pro_tips.tip: Sharp pegs and broken-in boots make outside-peg weighting easier to hold.
Lean the bike about half of the direction change (a 90-degree turn, roughly 45 degrees lean) as a rough rule; much more or less risks a low-side or high-side.

disagreements.point: Seat position: most say sit far forward; Racer X Braking and Set-Up notes sitting too far forward on the tank removes rear grip, and Jason Thomas moves back when the rear may spin under hard drive.

skills.note: New id for throttle and clutch control for traction in corners.

new_keys.key: Light to moderate drive helps the front steer and stay planted; heavy drive starts a slide that makes the front countersteer.
On exit, squeeze the clutch in slightly, then feed it out as you roll on to meter power to the rear.
Quick nips of the clutch cut drive faster and more precisely than the throttle when the bike is about to stand up or climb out.
Aim for enough power to drive out without wheelspin, swapping or a wheelie; each costs momentum.
Keep a finger on the front brake when getting on the gas hard; a light touch keeps the front down.
In a rut with the front light, stay on the power and modulate the clutch to hold traction.

new_faults.looks_like: Loud, roosting exit that is not actually fast.
new_faults.why: Feeling of speed from noise and spin.
new_faults.fix: Get on the gas earlier but smoother.

new_faults.looks_like: Lever pulled in at every exit to settle the bike, then let out.
new_faults.why: Habit; covering mistakes with the clutch.
new_faults.fix: Control the exit with throttle and body; ride sessions without the clutch.

new_faults.fault: Grabbing too much throttle out of a turn
new_faults.looks_like: Bike shoots wide across the track on exit.
new_faults.why: Big throttle before the bike is upright.
new_faults.fix: Roll on progressively as the bike comes up.

drills.name: No-clutch laps
drills.how: Ride laps without using the clutch except to stop.
drills.progression: Then laps without the rear brake; then both.
drills.done_when: You keep flow through the lap without stalling or bogging.

pro_tips.tip: On a four-stroke the clutch is mostly unnecessary if the corner is done right; keep a finger on it for small corrections.
Apply throttle by how much traction you feel once the bike is planted in the corner.

disagreements.point: How much clutch: Gary Bailey, Shane Booth and Racer X Corners use clutch on exit to meter drive; Andy Bowyer, MX-Gear and Cade Clason say use it as little as possible on a four-stroke; Shane Watts says feathering on flat-turn exits spins the rear.

gaps: YouTube coaching videos (Ryan Hughes, Ricky Carmichael University, Motocross Training Academy and others) returned only metadata or a bot-protection page; no transcripts, chapters or technique descriptions were readable. Gary Semics, Novik MX, Moto Mind, Brian Wheeler, Mike Brown, Ezra Lusk and Team Green content was not found in readable form.
youtube.com search pages are blocked for fetching; individual video pages found by search gave titles only.
Ryan Hughes 1-2-3 cornering method and "three parts of a turn / five steps": names known, content unknown.
Shane Watts DirtWise video library lists titles only (clutch control, throttle drills, standing cornering, race starts).
Transmoto starts how-to and inside-vs-outside corner pieces: only intro or teaser text readable.
Dirt Action deep-ruts video page: video only, no readable text.
Stoppies as a motocross braking skill: only one drill source (ADB); no MX coaching source on stoppies in race use.
Off-camber: no structured progressive drill found from a coach.
Line choice: little readable on inside vs outside choice by bike type or rider size.
Vital MX and Dirt Bike Magazine had few readable technique articles in this scope; Dirt Bike Magazine used only for Jeff Ward ruts.
Exact front/rear brake percentages vary by source and surface; treat as unknown beyond "front does most".
